label: copy-phase fed-back input b (from 2nd copied token on)
explanation: Token-specific feature: fires only in the copy phase when the fed-back input token is b (i.e., the model just output an original b), at steps from recall_idx 2 onward. It never fires in the original phase (even on b inputs) or at the delimiter, and almost never on non-b inputs. When b is the first original token and is fed back at recall_idx 1, it fires rarely and weakly (near zero). Activation is large and fairly uniform (median ~4.1); the weakest activations are b fed back early in the copy phase (recall_idx 1-2), and the strongest occur on b inputs near the end of long sequences, e.g. the final copy steps. Independent of out_tok, next_out, L, and digit count.

issues: No systematic counterexample found. On the test split there are 0 false positives (precision 1.0). All 1038 misses are b inputs at recall_idx 1 (b is the first original token and comes back right after <DEL>). Their activations are about 0.01-0.05 of max and hold only 0.1% of activation mass, which matches the explanation's claim that the feature rarely fires and stays near zero there.
The simpler predicate (phase 2 and input b) scores test F1 0.906, precision 0.829. Restricted to recall_idx==1, it scores dev precision 0.066. So the recall_idx >= 2 term is justified.

The magnitude claims check out: median 4.135. The lowest-quartile examples are b at recall_idx 1-2, around 0.54-0.63 of max. The top activations are b inputs at the last copy steps of length-9 sequences. Activation is flat across out_tok, next_out and prev_tok. Rate drops slightly as n_digits rises, but only in proportion to how often b occurs, so this is not a real dependence.
Minor: about 16 dev activations fire on inputs other than b (s, r, 3, y, ...). This is scattered noise, consistent with the claim that it almost never fires on other inputs.
